title: Forest Cover in India and the ISFR

cards.b:
Each new ISFR gives fresh numbers, and Prelims often asks about the state with the highest forest cover or the target in the National Forest Policy. Mains asks whether cover really means healthy forest.

This lesson holds the definitions and the figures with their years.

The India State of Forest Report (ISFR) is published every two years by the Forest Survey of India (FSI), Dehradun (set up in 1981). It uses satellite data (Resourcesat) and field checks. It reports forest cover (all land over one hectare with tree canopy density above 10 percent, whatever the owner) and tree cover (patches under one hectare, outside forest).

Recorded forest area is a legal term for land recorded as forest in revenue records. It is different from cover.

• Very Dense Forest (VDF): canopy density 70 percent and above.
  • Moderately Dense Forest (MDF): 40 to 70 percent.
  • Open Forest (OF): 10 to 40 percent.
  • Scrub: below 10 percent.

The ISFR also reports mangrove cover, carbon stock in forests, bamboo area, and forest fire alerts. India reports its forest carbon sink to the UNFCCC, and a stated goal is an additional carbon sink of 2.5 to 3 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2030.

• ISFR 2021: forest cover about 7.13 lakh sq km, 21.71 percent of area; tree cover 2.91 percent; total about 24.62 percent.
  • ISFR 2023: forest cover about 7.15 lakh sq km (21.76 percent); tree cover 3.41 percent; total about 25.17 percent.

Madhya Pradesh has the largest forest area. Mizoram has the highest percentage of forest cover among states (above 84 percent in ISFR 2021). Among Union Territories, Lakshadweep is highest. States showing large gains in recent reports include Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Telangana, while losses are seen in the North-East.

The National Forest Policy 1952 and 1988 set the goal of 33 percent of land under forest or tree cover, with 66 percent in hills. The 1988 policy puts conservation first and calls for people's involvement (Joint Forest Management, 1990). The Green India Mission (under NAPCC) aims to increase and improve forest cover. The Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016 funds replanting. India's Bonn Challenge pledge is 26 million hectares of degraded land to be restored by 2030.

Champion and Seth (1968) classified Indian forests into 16 major types. Tropical moist deciduous and tropical dry deciduous forests cover the largest area. Tropical wet evergreen forests are found in the Western Ghats, the North-East and the Andaman. Sal and teak are major timber species. Mangroves and montane types complete the list.

Plantations and monocultures can raise "cover" without raising biodiversity.

The Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel (Madhav Gadgil, 2011) suggested the whole range be an ecologically sensitive area with three zones. The High-Level Working Group (K. Kasturirangan, 2013) cut this to 37 percent of the area (about 59,940 sq km) as ESA across six states. States opposed both, citing farmers and mining.

MoEFCC has issued repeated draft notifications on the ESA since 2014. A final notification is still debated (as of recent years).

Critics say the ISFR counts plantations, orchards and even coconut groves as forest, so the rise masks the loss of natural forest. Open forests are growing but VDF area changes are small. Diversion of forest for mines and dams is a leading concern, and the Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act 2023 added more debates on this.

About 300 million people live near forests, and Non-Timber Forest Produce (NTFP) is a key livelihood for tribal families. Forest fire is a big risk in Uttarakhand and Odisha during summer. FSI sends fire alerts to forest staff using satellite data.

Forest fire alerts, NTFP income and the 300 million forest-edge population are useful lines for a Mains answer.

Prelims-style: "Which state has the highest forest cover in percentage?" (Mizoram). "Which body publishes ISFR?" (FSI). "National Forest Policy 1988 target?" (33 percent).

Mains-style: "Examine the trends in India's forest cover. Does an increase in cover mean better forests?" Structure: ISFR figures; types and density; plantations versus natural forests; policy tools; threats; way forward.
